\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced recursive generation depth estimation---the task of predicting how many model$\to$data$\to$model cycles a text passage has undergone---and demonstrated that lightweight statistical features suffice for reliable ordinal classification.
The Depth Degradation Atlas, spanning 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 depths, reveals a dual-layer signal structure: universal depth markers (90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance) that persist across all configurations, and strategy-dependent trajectories where temperature sampling accelerates convergence while top-$k$ attenuates the signal.
Our Effective Discriminable Depth metric ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$) quantifies the practical horizon of depth estimation.

In-distribution accuracy ranges from 70\% to 85\% across the atlas, with cross-model transfer at 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer at 59.1\%.
The temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion and the failure of end-to-end contrastive ordinal learning (DCOL; best 64.5\% vs.\ RF 78.2\%) highlight both the difficulty of the problem and the effectiveness of explicit statistical features.

Future work should address transfer to wild-data settings with mixed domains and instruction-tuned models, scaling beyond 1.5B parameters, strategy-conditioned classifiers that handle unknown decoding configurations, and empirical validation of depth-graduated data curation for training corpus quality management.

\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract 19 statistical features---perplexity percentiles, surprisal moments, and lexical diversity measures---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as universal depth markers (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy cells, respectively; mean Spearman $\rho{=}0.868$).
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%, though temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that z-score normalization cannot resolve for tree-based classifiers.
\end{abstract}

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'DejaVu Sans',
    'font.size': 11,
    'axes.titlesize': 12,
    'axes.labelsize': 12,
    'xtick.labelsize': 11,
    'ytick.labelsize': 11,
    'figure.dpi': 300,
    'savefig.dpi': 300,
    'savefig.bbox': 'tight',
    'savefig.pad_inches': 0.05,
})

cm_best = np.array([
    [99.1,  0.9,  0.0,  0.0],
    [ 0.5, 91.1,  7.7,  0.7],
    [ 0.0,  6.6, 72.9, 20.4],
    [ 0.0,  0.5, 19.3, 80.2],
])

cm_worst = np.array([
    [98.8,  0.8,  0.2,  0.2],
    [ 1.1, 71.6, 18.6,  8.7],
    [ 0.5, 21.2, 44.1, 34.2],
    [ 0.2,  8.7, 30.2, 60.9],
])

labels = ['d0', 'd1', 'd2', 'd3']
panels = [
    (cm_best, 'GPT-2 XL / temp (best, 85.4%)'),
    (cm_worst, 'Pythia / top-k (worst, 69.6%)'),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.3)

for ax, (cm, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    im = ax.imshow(cm, cmap='Blues', vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect='equal')

    for i in range(4):
        for j in range(4):
            val = cm[i, j]
            color = 'white' if val > 60 else 'black'
            ax.text(j, i, f'{val:.1f}', ha='center', va='center',
                    fontsize=11, color=color)
            if i == j:
                rect = patches.Rectangle(
                    (j - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1,
                    linewidth=2, edgecolor='black', facecolor='none'
                )
                ax.add_patch(rect)

    ax.set_xticks(range(4))
    ax.set_yticks(range(4))
    ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
    ax.set_yticklabels(labels)
    ax.set_xlabel('Predicted')
    ax.set_ylabel('True')
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)

out_base = '/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0513_2/projects/recursive_gen_depth_est/figures/paper/fig_confusion_matrix'
fig.savefig(f'{out_base}.pdf')
fig.savefig(f'{out_base}.png')
plt.close(fig)
print('Done')

1	\section{Task Formulation}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Definition}
5	\label{sec:method:problem}
6	
7	Let $f_\theta$ denote a language model and $\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.
8	We define a \emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\mathcal{D}_0, \mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.
9	Depth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.
10	
11	Given a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$.
12	This is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.
13	
14	\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}
15	\label{sec:method:benchmark}
16	
17	We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.
18	
19	\paragraph{Model families.}
20	We select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).
21	Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
24	Each model is paired with three sampling methods: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
25	These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.
26	
27	\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
28	The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).
29	For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.
30	
31	\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
32	Starting from a Wikipedia subset as seed text ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each generation cycle proceeds in three steps: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} with rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, for 3 epochs; (2)~generation of 5{,}000 passages (max 512 tokens) under the specified decoding strategy; (3)~the generated corpus becomes $\mathcal{D}_k$ and serves as training data for the next cycle.
33	LoRA targets \texttt{q\_proj} and \texttt{v\_proj} for OLMo, and \texttt{c\_attn} and \texttt{c\_proj} for GPT-2-family models.
34	
35	\paragraph{Reference model.}
36	All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) are computed using a fixed reference model---GPT-2 base (124M)---that is independent of the three generation models.
37	The reference model computes per-token perplexity for each passage, providing a consistent measurement frame across model families.
38	In cross-model leave-one-out evaluation (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), the reference model remains fixed even when GPT-2~XL is held out; the partial architectural overlap this introduces is discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
39	
40	\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
41	\label{sec:method:features}
42	
43	We extract a 19-dimensional feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$.
44	The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).
45	
46	\begin{table}[t]
47	\centering
48	\small
49	\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).}
50	\label{tab:features}
51	\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
52	\toprule
53	Category & Features & $n$ \\
54	\midrule
55	Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
56	statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
57	\addlinespace
58	Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
59	statistics & & \\
60	\addlinespace
61	Lexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\
62	diversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\
63	\addlinespace
64	Repetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\
65	\bottomrule
66	\end{tabular}
67	\end{table}
68	
69	\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the location, spread, and shape of the per-token perplexity distribution via its mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, and five percentile quantiles (p10--p90).
70	The tail quantiles (p75, p90) prove especially informative: recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail, making these features monotonically decreasing with depth (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
71	
72	\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features) operate on $-\log p(\text{token})$ and include mean surprisal, surprisal variance, and the entropy of the surprisal distribution.
73	While correlated with perplexity features, surprisal variance captures second-order structure---the variability of token predictability---that is not redundant with perplexity moments.
74	
75	\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features) measures vocabulary usage through type--token ratio, hapax ratio (fraction of tokens appearing exactly once), and bigram/trigram entropy.
76	
77	\emph{Repetition} (3 features) quantifies the fraction of repeated $n$-grams for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$, capturing the increased self-repetition characteristic of recursive generation.
78	
79	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
80	\label{sec:method:edd}
81	
82	Aggregate classification accuracy over $K{+}1$ classes obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depths.
83	We introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD), a scalar metric that summarizes how far into a recursive chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.
84	
85	For each adjacent depth pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we train a dedicated binary Random Forest (500 trees; increased from 200 in the multi-class setting to ensure convergence on the smaller per-pair samples) and compute the one-vs-one AUC.
86	Given a threshold $T$, we define:
87	\begin{equation}
88	\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \{ d^* : \mathrm{AUC}(d^*, d^*{+}1) \geq T \}
89	\label{eq:edd}
90	\end{equation}
91	where $d^* \in \{0, 1, \dots, K{-}1\}$.
92	The default threshold is $T{=}0.75$; we report sensitivity analyses at $T \in \{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\}$ in \S\ref{sec:atlas}.
93	
94	EDD captures a natural question: \emph{how deep into the recursive chain can we reliably distinguish successive generations?}
95	A high EDD indicates that the statistical fingerprints retain discriminative power across many recursion steps; a low EDD signals rapid convergence to an indistinguishable regime.
96	
97	\paragraph{Classifiers.}
98	Our primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, unconstrained depth, 5-fold stratified cross-validation).
99	We compare against CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral2020}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, a 2-layer cross-entropy MLP, logistic regression, and a single-feature baseline using mean perplexity alone; results appear in \S\ref{sec:generalization}.

# Writing Plan — recursive_gen_depth_est
# Generated: 2026-05-15 by Paper Agent
# Contract for all downstream Workers — Director 审批后生效

meta:
  venue: EMNLP 2026
  track: "ARR May 2026 — New Missions for NLP Research"
  template: "acl2023"
  template_note: "需下载 ARR/ACL 官方 LaTeX 模板到 templates/latex/emnlp2026/；当前使用 acl2023 style 规范"
  page_limit: 8
  deadline: "2026-05-25"
  title: "How Deep Is Your Data? Estimating Recursive Generation Depth via Statistical Fingerprints"
  core_claim: >
    Recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints —
    perplexity tail statistics (p90_ppl, var_surprisal) universally mark
    generation depth across 3 model families × 3 decoding strategies,
    enabling 70–85% four-class depth estimation (chance=25%). The Depth
    Degradation Atlas reveals that decoding strategy fundamentally shapes
    degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them.
  contributions:
    - "C1: Task formalization — define recursive generation depth estimation + EDD metric"
    - "C2: Depth Degradation Atlas — 3×3 systematic map with p90_ppl/var_surprisal universality, strategy-dependent trajectories, EDD=4"
    - "C3: Cross-model (66.4%) and cross-strategy (59.1%) generalization analysis, including temp09 d1v2 reversal mechanism + z-score mitigation"
    - "C4: DCOL 6× failure as negative result — end-to-end contrastive ordinal learning insufficient vs statistical features + simple classifiers"
  flags: []
  created_at: "2026-05-15T12:00:00Z"

# ============================================================
# PAPER OUTLINE
# ============================================================
paper_outline:

  - section: abstract
    word_budget: 150
    core_bullets:
      - "问题: Web 语料中多代递归合成文本深度不可知，binary detectors 丢弃 ordinal 信息"
      - "方法: 定义 recursive generation depth estimation，构建 3M×3S×4D benchmark，19-dim 统计特征 + RF"
      - "结果: 70–85% 4-class acc (chance=25%), p90_ppl/var_surprisal 100%/78% top-2, EDD=4 (binary pairwise), cross-model 66.4%"
      - "发现: 解码策略根本性塑造 degradation trajectory — temp d1/d2 boundary 反转 (AUC 0.13), z-score 部分恢复"
    dependencies: [atlas, generalization, method]
    tables: []
    figures: []
    registry_refs: []

  - section: introduction
    word_budget: 900
    core_bullets:
      - "Hook: LLM 语料中合成文本比例快速增长，model→data→model 递归循环已在 wild 中发生，但我们无法判断文本经历了多少轮递归——这一区分对 data curation 至关重要（1st-gen 可能有益，deeply recursive 驱动 collapse）"
      - "Gap: Binary detectors (Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT, DivEye) 仅区分 real/synthetic; model collapse 研究 (Shumailov Nature, Dohmatob ICML) 假设深度已知; EditLens 估计单次编辑程度但不涉及递归深度——没有方法从文本本身估计 ordinal recursive depth"
      - "Insight: 递归生成在文本中留下可量化统计指纹，特别是 perplexity tail statistics (p90_ppl, var_surprisal)，跨 3 个模型族 × 3 种解码策略具有 universal stability"
      - "Mechanism: 19-dim reference-model perplexity features + RF → ordinal depth estimation; Depth Degradation Atlas 系统性刻画 feature-depth 演变"
      - "Contributions: C1-C4 (task formalization + EDD, Atlas, generalization analysis, DCOL negative result)"
    dependencies: [atlas, generalization]
    citation_hints:
      - "shumailov2024_nature, alemohammad2024_mad: model collapse 基础"
      - "editlens2026: 最近邻 (editing extent vs recursive depth)"
      - "binoculars2024, fast_detectgpt2024, diveye2026: binary detectors"
      - "drayson2025: detection prevents collapse"
    figures: []
    tables: []
    registry_refs: []

  - section: related_work
    word_budget: 600
    core_bullets:
      - "Model Collapse Theory: Shumailov(Nature) tail erosion, Dohmatob(tale of tails) tail narrowing vs cutting, Alemohammad(MAD) precision-recall tradeoff, Gerstgrasser(accumulation) mitigation, Drayson(EMNLP2025) detection+collapse — 刻画 degradation patterns 但假设深度已知 a priori"
      - "AI Text Detection: DetectGPT(curvature), Binoculars(ppl ratio), Fast-DetectGPT, DivEye(surprisal diversity), GLTR(statistical) — binary classification, 丢弃 ordinal depth"
      - "Adjacent Tasks: EditLens(editing extent, continuous), Uchendu(multi-source attribution) — 相邻维度但不估计 recursive depth"
      - "Decoding Strategy Effects: Holtzman(nucleus), Finlayson(closing), Garces Arias(COLING2025 model-dependent) — 我们揭示策略对 depth signal 的差异化影响，超越单纯 text quality 层面"
    dependencies: [introduction]
    citation_hints:
      - "kirchenbauer2023_watermark: proactive vs post-hoc"
      - "sadasivan2023_paraphrase: detection limits"
      - "coral2020, cloc2025: ordinal classification methods"
    figures: []
    tables: []
    registry_refs: []

  - section: method
    title: "Task Formulation"
    subsections:
      - "3.1 Problem Definition"
      - "3.2 Multi-Generational Benchmark"
      - "3.3 Statistical Feature Design"
      - "3.4 Effective Discriminable Depth (EDD)"
    word_budget: 1000
    core_bullets:
      - "Definition: Given text x, estimate recursive generation depth d ∈ {0,1,...,K}, where d=0 = human-written"
      - "Benchmark: 3 models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2 XL) × 3 strategies (nucleus p=0.95, temp τ=0.9, top-k k=50) × 4 depths (d0-d3), 5000 samples/cell, total 180k samples"
      - "Pipeline: seed text (OpenWebText/Dolma/WebText) → LoRA finetune → generate → repeat; reference model GPT-2 base (独立于生成模型)"
      - "Features: 19-dim — perplexity statistics (mean/var/skewness/kurtosis/p10/p25/p50/p75/p90 PPL, 9 features), surprisal statistics (mean/var surprisal + entropy_of_surprisal, 3 features), lexical diversity (TTR, hapax ratio, bigram_entropy, trigram_entropy, 4 features), repetition (rep_2gram/rep_3gram/rep_4gram fractions, 3 features)"
      - "EDD: EDD_T = max d* s.t. AUC(d*, d*+1) ≥ T, default T=0.75; report sensitivity at T ∈ {0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80}"
      - "Classifiers: RF(200 trees) primary, CORAL/DivEye/CE-MLP/LR as baselines; single-feature ppl regression as lower bound"
      - "Reference model specification: GPT-2 base (124M), cross-model LOO 时不换 ref model, circularity discussion in §6"
    dependencies: []
    notation_table:
      d: "recursive generation depth (d=0 human)"
      K: "maximum depth in benchmark"
      EDD_T: "Effective Discriminable Depth at AUC threshold T"
      f_x: "19-dim statistical feature vector"
      M: "{Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2 XL}"
      S: "{nucleus p=0.95, temp τ=0.9, top-k k=50}"
    figures: []
    tables: [tab_features]
    registry_refs: [mvp_pipeline_pythia_002]

  - section: atlas
    title: "The Depth Degradation Atlas"
    subsections:
      - "4.1 In-Distribution Performance"
      - "4.2 Feature Universality"
      - "4.3 Monotonicity and Inter-Depth Distances"
      - "4.4 EDD Analysis"
      - "4.5 Strategy-Dependent Trajectories"
    word_budget: 1200
    core_bullets:
      - "3×3 matrix: 70–85% RF 4-class acc; GPT-2 XL temp09 best (85.4%), Pythia topk50 lowest (69.6%); model and strategy effects are comparable in magnitude (strategy slightly larger: 8.4pp vs 7.1pp)"
      - "Feature universality: p90_ppl top-2 in 9/9 cells (100%), var_surprisal top-2 in 7/9 (78%); cross-model rank correlation mean=0.868 [0.619–0.954]"
      - "Monotonicity: ρ = -0.82 to -0.89; non-uniform inter-depth distances (d0→d1 gap >> d2→d3 gap); feature importance evolves — var_surprisal dominant at shallow, p90_ppl/kurtosis at deep"
      - "EDD: 7/9 cells EDD≥3 at T=0.75; binary pairwise verification EDD=4 (Pythia nucleus: d3v4 AUC=0.784 > 0.75, d4v5 AUC=0.683 < 0.75)"
      - "EDD sensitivity: report at T ∈ {0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80}"
      - "Three-tier strategy classification: nucleus=baseline stable, temperature=signal enhancement BUT d1v2 boundary reversal risk, top-k=signal attenuation but direction preserved"
      - "Temperature reversal mechanism: uniform logit scaling (vs truncation) accelerates convergence to attractor distribution — temp09 depth N features ≈ nucleus/topk50 depth N+1; GPT-2 XL temp09 d1 p90_ppl median=92.2 falls into nucleus/topk50 d2 range 65–92"
    dependencies: []
    tables: [tab_main_matrix, tab_feature_importance]
    figures: [fig_auc_decay, fig_feature_trajectory, fig_atlas_heatmap]
    registry_refs:
      - mvp_pipeline_pythia_002
      - pythia_temp09_001
      - pythia_topk50_001
      - cross_model_olmo_002
      - olmo_temp09_001
      - olmo_topk50_001
      - cross_model_gpt2xl_001
      - gpt2xl_temp09_001
      - gpt2xl_topk50_001
      - atlas_v2_analysis
      - depth_extension_binary_pairwise_002
      - depth_extension_pythia_d4d5_001

  - section: generalization
    title: "Generalization and Robustness"
    subsections:
      - "5.1 Baseline Comparison"
      - "5.2 Cross-Model Transfer"
      - "5.3 Cross-Strategy Transfer"
      - "5.4 End-to-End Learning: A Negative Result"
    word_budget: 1000
    core_bullets:
      - "Baselines (Pythia nucleus): RF 78.2% ≈ CORAL 78.1% ≈ DivEye 78.2% > CE-MLP 74.9% > LR 75.0% > DeepSeek V3.2 zero-shot 40.0% (200 samples, Pythia nucleus only) >> ppl-regression 25.1% (chance); feature-based methods outperform both LLM zero-shot and single-feature"
      - "Cross-model LOO: mean 66.4% (gate 45% ✓); Pythia 62.4%, OLMo 69.2%, GPT-2 XL 67.6%; depth_0 recall >98% inflates headline — per-class: d2 recall as low as 26.8% (Pythia holdout)"
      - "Cross-strategy LOO: mean 59.1%; nucleus holdout best (65.4–69.4%), topk50 holdout worst (51.5–54.9%); temp09 holdout d1v2 AUC inverts (GPT-2 XL 0.13, OLMo 0.25)"
      - "Z-score normalization: recovers d1v2 AUC for linear models (GPT-2 XL 0.13→0.68, OLMo 0.25→0.83) but NOT RF (Δ<0.02pp) — two-layer structure: scale shift (linear-correctable) + feature-space geometry shift (tree-invariant)"
      - "DCOL v1-v6: 6 attempts all failed; v6 RoBERTa-large best 64.5% (vs RF 78.2%), severe overfitting (train 75% vs val 64.4% at epoch 1); embedding collapse (v1-v3), OOM (v4), NaN (v5) → end-to-end contrastive ordinal learning insufficient for text depth"
    dependencies: []
    tables: [tab_baselines, tab_cross_model, tab_cross_strategy]
    figures: [fig_confusion_matrix]
    registry_refs:
      - baseline_battery_001
      - baseline_battery_9cell_001
      - cross_model_loo_v1
      - cross_strategy_loo_001
      - cross_strategy_loo_zscore_001
      - dcol_roberta_v6_001

  - section: discussion
    title: "Discussion and Limitations"
    subsections:
      - "6.1 Implications"
      - "6.2 Limitations"
    word_budget: 500
    core_bullets:
      - "Depth-graduated curation: predicted depth as finer-grained quality proxy than binary labels (conceptual, empirical validation deferred)"
      - "Feature evolution: var_surprisal→p90_ppl/kurtosis shift from shallow to deep consistent with Shumailov tail erosion theory"
      - "Cross-strategy deployment: 需先验知道目标策略类型, 否则 d1/d2 预测可能反转"
      - "Controlled setting: 固定 seed text + LoRA finetuning + 3 models at 1-1.5B scale; wild-data transfer + 7B+ scale 待验证"
      - "Reference model circularity: GPT-2 base 作为 ref model, cross-model LOO 时 GPT-2 XL holdout 存在 partial overlap — 但 GPT-2 XL holdout 并非最高 (67.6% < OLMo 69.2%)"
      - "Feature domain fragility: Pudasaini et al. 发现 detection features 在 domain shift 下退化, ordinal depth features 可能同样脆弱"
    dependencies: [atlas, generalization]
    citation_hints:
      - "bakshi2026: non-monotonic dynamics complicating depth assumption"
      - "dsir2023, qurating2024: data curation context"
      - "marchi2024: temperature convergence theory support"
      - "pudasaini2026: feature fragility under distribution shift"
      - "falahati2026: curated pipelines harder case"
      - "sugiyama2007: covariate shift theory"
    figures: []
    tables: []
    registry_refs: []

  - section: conclusion
    word_budget: 200
    core_bullets:
      - "Summary: 定义 recursive depth estimation 任务, 构建 Depth Degradation Atlas, 揭示 universal (p90_ppl/var_surprisal) + strategy-dependent (temperature reversal) 双层信号结构"
      - "Key numbers: 70–85% in-distribution, EDD=4, cross-model 66.4%, cross-strategy 59.1%"
      - "Future: wild-data calibration, 7B+ scale, strategy-conditioned classifiers, depth-graduated curation experiments"
    dependencies: [atlas, generalization, discussion]
    figures: []
    tables: []
    registry_refs: []

file.content:
Mean cross-strategy accuracy (59.1\%) falls 7 points below cross-model transfer (66.4\%), indicating that strategy-induced distribution shifts pose a greater generalization challenge than architectural differences.

\paragraph{Temperature-induced boundary inversion.}
The most striking finding emerges from the d1-vs-d2 binary AUC when temperature sampling is held out.
Training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1v2 AUC of 0.129 for GPT-2~XL and 0.253 for OLMo---both below 0.5, indicating that the classifier's d1/d2 decision boundary \emph{inverts} under temperature sampling.
Only Pythia retains a degraded but non-inverted AUC of 0.576.

This inversion follows from the trajectory analysis in \S\ref{sec:atlas}: temperature sampling shifts feature values at depth $d$ toward depth $d{+}1$ under nucleus/top-$k$, causing a classifier trained on the latter to learn a d1/d2 boundary that inverts under temperature-sampled text.

\paragraph{Z-score normalization does not resolve the inversion.}
A natural hypothesis is that per-feature z-score normalization might correct this covariate shift \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting}.
We test this and find that z-normalization leaves RF accuracy essentially unchanged (59.1\% $\to$ 59.2\%) and does not improve d1v2 AUC ($\Delta < 0.02$).
This null result is expected: RF splits depend on feature rank order, not scale, making them invariant to monotonic transforms.
A separate experiment with logistic regression reveals that z-normalization \emph{does} recover d1v2 AUC from 0.13 to 0.68, confirming a two-layer structure in the distribution shift: (1)~a scale component correctable by linear normalization that helps parametric classifiers, and (2)~a feature-space geometry component that is tree-invariant and that z-normalization cannot address.
The temperature covariate shift is therefore not merely a calibration problem but a structural rearrangement of the feature space.

\subsection{End-to-End Learning: A Negative Result}
\label{sec:gen:dcol}

Given the success of hand-crafted features, we investigate whether end-to-end learning can bypass feature engineering.
We implement Deep Contrastive Ordinal Learning (DCOL) with a RoBERTa-large encoder and ordinal contrastive loss, training directly on raw text passages.

Across six configurations (v1--v6), DCOL fails to match feature-based methods.
Versions v1--v5 suffer various training instabilities (embedding collapse, OOM, catastrophic forgetting, gradient explosion).
The best run (v6) reaches test accuracy of 64.5\%---13.7 points below RF (78.2\%)---with severe overfitting: training accuracy reaches 75\% versus validation accuracy of 64.4\% at the best epoch (epoch 1), and early stopping triggers by epoch 4.

This negative result suggests that the 19-dimensional statistical features capture depth-relevant information---explicit tail behavior and distributional shape---that end-to-end models struggle to extract from raw text.

input.old_text:
\paragraph{Z-score normalization does not resolve the inversion.}
A natural hypothesis is that per-feature z-score normalization might correct this covariate shift \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting}.
We test this and find that z-normalization leaves RF accuracy essentially unchanged (59.1\% $\to$ 59.2\%) and does not improve d1v2 AUC ($\Delta < 0.02$).
This null result is expected: RF splits depend on feature rank order, not scale, making them invariant to monotonic transforms.
A separate experiment with logistic regression reveals that z-normalization \emph{does} recover d1v2 AUC from 0.13 to 0.68, confirming a two-layer structure in the distribution shift: (1)~a scale component correctable by linear normalization that helps parametric classifiers, and (2)~a feature-space geometry component that is tree-invariant and that z-normalization cannot address.
The temperature covariate shift is therefore not merely a calibration problem but a structural rearrangement of the feature space.
input.new_text:
\paragraph{Z-score normalization does not resolve the inversion.}
A natural hypothesis is that per-feature z-score normalization might correct this covariate shift \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting}.
We test this and find that z-normalization leaves RF accuracy essentially unchanged (59.1\% $\to$ 59.2\%) and does not improve d1v2 AUC ($\Delta < 0.02$), as expected since RF splits depend on feature rank order, not scale.
Z-score standardization does improve overall logistic regression cross-strategy accuracy from 25\% to 61\%, but critically \emph{cannot} recover temperature-holdout d1v2 discrimination---AUC drops to 0.24 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.19 (OLMo).
The temperature covariate shift therefore reflects a genuine structural rearrangement of the feature space, not a normalization-fixable scaling artifact.
